home.title: What you’ll actually take home
home.seoTitle: Pay Calculator Australia 2026–27: Take-Home Pay After Tax
home.description: Free Australian pay calculator for 2026–27. Your take-home pay after tax, Medicare and HECS-HELP, plus super, per week, fortnight, month and year.
home.lede: Type your pay the way it’s written in your contract or job ad. You’ll see what lands in your account after tax, Medicare and any HECS-HELP, using the ATO’s 2026–27 rates.

faq.q: Is this the same as what’s on my payslip?
faq.a: Close, but not to the dollar. Your employer withholds tax each pay using the ATO’s withholding tables, which round each pay period. This calculator works out the tax for the whole year and divides it by 52, 26 or 12. Any difference usually comes back (or is owed) when you lodge your tax return.

faq.q: Which tax rates does it use?
faq.a: The 2026–27 rates for Australian residents: nothing on the first $18,200, then 15%, 30%, 37% and 45%. The 15% rate is new from 1 July 2026 (it was 16%), and it falls to 14% from 1 July 2027.

faq.q: Does it include the low income tax offset?
faq.a: Yes. If you earn under about $66,667 the offset (up to $700) comes off your tax automatically. It can bring your tax to nil, but it can’t be paid out as a refund on its own.

Some job ads quote a package that already includes your employer’s 12% super. Pick “Includes super” and the calculator works out the salary part first. If your contract says your salary is “plus super”, leave it on “Super on top”.

Tick it if you still owe a study loan (HECS-HELP, VET Student Loan, Australian Apprenticeship Support Loan or similar). From 2025–26 repayments are only on the part of your income above the threshold, which is $69,528 for 2026–27.

The Medicare levy surcharge (if you earn over the threshold without private hospital cover), salary sacrifice, deductions, other tax offsets, and family Medicare thresholds. It also assumes you’re an Australian resident for tax who claims the tax-free threshold from one job.

faq.q: Is anything I type sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The sums run in your browser. We don’t store or see what you type.

salary.title: Salaries after tax in Australia
salary.seoTitle: Salary After Tax Australia 2026–27: Every Salary From $20k to $300k
salary.description: Take-home pay for every salary from $20,000 to $300,000 in Australia for 2026–27: per year, month, fortnight and week, with tax and Medicare worked out.
salary.lede: Pick a salary to see the take-home pay for 2026–27, worked out line by line. Every figure assumes an Australian resident claiming the tax-free threshold, with super paid on top.

tax-brackets.title: Australian tax brackets 2026–27
tax-brackets.seoTitle: Tax Brackets Australia 2026–27: Rates, Thresholds & What Changed
tax-brackets.description: The 2026–27 Australian resident tax rates and thresholds, what changed from 2025–26 (16% to 15%), what changes in 2027–28, and how the brackets actually work.
tax-brackets.lede: From 1 July 2026, the second tax rate dropped from 16% to 15%. The thresholds didn’t move. Here’s the full table and what it means for your pay.
how: Tax brackets only apply to the part of your income inside each bracket. Earning one dollar more never makes your whole income taxed at a higher rate.
On a $60,000 salary, the first $18,200 is tax-free, the next $26,800 is taxed at 15%, and the last $15,000 at 30%. That’s $8,520 before the low income tax offset and the Medicare levy.
The Medicare levy (2% for most people) is on top of these rates, and so are HECS-HELP repayments if you have a study loan.

faq.q: How much do I save from the 15% rate?
faq.a: If you earn $45,000 or more, the cut from 16% to 15% saves you $268 a year (1% of the $26,800 between $18,200 and $45,000). Below $45,000 you save 1% of whatever you earn over $18,200.
The same rate falls again, from 15% to 14%, from 1 July 2027. That’s another saving of up to $268 a year.

faq.q: Do these rates apply to working holiday makers or non-residents?
faq.a: No. Non-residents and working holiday makers have their own rates, with no tax-free threshold. This page and our calculator cover Australian residents for tax only.

hecs-help-repayments.title: HECS-HELP repayments 2026–27
hecs-help-repayments.seoTitle: HECS-HELP Repayment Thresholds 2026–27: How Much You’ll Repay
hecs-help-repayments.description: 2026–27 HECS-HELP and study loan repayment thresholds, the new marginal system explained, and how much comes out of your pay at every income.
hecs-help-repayments.lede: Since 2025–26, study loan repayments are only charged on the part of your income above the threshold, like a tax bracket. For 2026–27 you repay nothing until your income passes $69,528.
how: Your repayment is worked out on your repayment income: your taxable income plus a few extras such as reportable fringe benefits, reportable super contributions and net investment losses. For most employees it’s simply their taxable income.
Between $69,529 and $129,717 you repay 15 cents for each dollar over $69,528. Above that, it’s 17 cents on each extra dollar, on top of $9,028.
From $186,051 the rule changes: you repay 10% of your whole repayment income, not just the part above a threshold.
Your employer takes repayments out of each pay once you tick the study loan box on your tax file number declaration. The final amount is settled when you lodge your tax return.

faq.a: HELP (including HECS-HELP and FEE-HELP), VET Student Loans, Australian Apprenticeship Support Loans and the other study and training support loans the ATO collects. They all use the same thresholds.

faq.q: Does paying it back early help?
faq.a: Voluntary repayments reduce the debt straight away. The debt is indexed each 1 June, so paying before then means less indexation. Whether it’s worth it depends on your other debts and savings goals.

faq.q: Why did my repayments drop in 2025–26?
faq.a: The system changed from a percentage of your whole income to a percentage of the part above the threshold, and the threshold rose to $67,000. Most people repay less each year under the new rules.

how-we-calculate.title: How we calculate
how-we-calculate.description: The rates, sources and assumptions behind MyPayCalc’s take-home pay figures for 2026–27, and what the calculator doesn’t cover.
paragraphs: Every rate on this site comes from the Australian Taxation Office or the legislation that set it. We list each source below with the date we last checked it. When the ATO publishes new figures, we update them and re-run our checks.

We work out your tax for the whole income year, then divide it by 52, 26 or 12 for weekly, fortnightly and monthly figures. Payslips use the ATO’s withholding tables instead, which round each pay, so your payslip can differ by a few dollars. The difference is settled at tax time.

The steps are: your taxable income (your salary, not counting employer super); income tax at the 2026–27 resident rates; minus the low income tax offset; plus the Medicare levy at 2%, reduced for low incomes; plus study loan repayments if you have one. What’s left is your take-home pay.

For the Medicare levy we use the latest published low-income thresholds, which are for 2025–26 ($28,011 and $35,013 for singles). The government usually sets the 2026–27 thresholds in the May Budget, after the year has started, and we’ll update them then.

Super is your employer’s 12% super guarantee on top of your salary. If you pick “Includes super”, we take the 12% out of the package first. For 2026–27, employers don’t have to pay super on earnings above $270,830 a year.

Not included: the Medicare levy surcharge, family Medicare thresholds, salary sacrifice, deductions, offsets other than the low income tax offset, non-residents and working holiday makers, and second jobs where you don’t claim the tax-free threshold.

We test the calculator against figures worked by hand from the ATO’s tables every time the site is built. If you spot a figure that looks wrong, please [tell us](/contact) and we’ll check it the same week.
This is general information, not tax advice. For your own situation, the ATO or a registered tax agent can help.

about.title: About MyPayCalc
about.description: Who runs MyPayCalc, why it exists and how we keep the figures right.
paragraphs: MyPayCalc is a free Australian pay calculator. It answers one question well: how much of my pay will I actually keep?
It’s run by Independent Media Network Pty Ltd, a small Melbourne company owned by Simon Farrugia. Simon spent years working in employment services before starting his own small businesses.
We keep it simple: no sign-up, nothing you type leaves your browser, and every rate is sourced from the ATO and dated. You can see exactly [how we calculate](/how-we-calculate).
Found a mistake or want a feature? [Get in touch](/contact).

contact.title: Contact
contact.description: How to contact MyPayCalc about a figure that looks wrong, a feature idea or anything else.
paragraphs: Email hello@mypaycalc.com.au. We read every message and usually reply within two working days.
Spotted a figure that looks wrong? Tell us the salary and options you used, and what you expected. We check every report against the ATO’s tables.

Feature ideas are welcome too. The calculator started with the questions people ask most (take-home pay, HECS-HELP and super), and we add what readers ask for next, such as part-time hours, a second job or salary sacrifice.
We can’t give personal tax advice. For that, contact the ATO or a registered tax agent.

how-we-make-money.title: How we make money
how-we-make-money.description: How MyPayCalc pays for itself, and why it never changes the figures.
paragraphs: MyPayCalc is free. We plan to show clearly marked ads on some pages to pay for running it.
Ads never change the figures. The maths comes only from the ATO’s published rates, and we test it every time the site is built.

We don’t sell your data, and there’s nothing to sell: the calculator runs in your browser and we never see the pay you type. We also don’t take payment to change a result, rank a product higher or write about a company.
If we ever link to a product that pays us when you sign up, we’ll say so next to the link.

privacy-policy.title: Privacy policy
privacy-policy.description: MyPayCalc’s privacy policy: what we collect (very little) and what we never collect.
paragraphs: The calculator runs entirely in your browser. The pay, options and results you enter are never sent to us or anyone else, and we don’t store them.
If we add website analytics or ads, they may use cookies to count visits and show ads. We’ll update this policy before that happens, and you’ll be able to see and change your choices.
If you email us, we use your email address only to reply.
MyPayCalc is run by Independent Media Network Pty Ltd, Melbourne. Questions about privacy: hello@mypaycalc.com.au.
